title: The Ascent to Root
intro: THE ASCENT TO ROOT
The mainframe is failing, and root — its keeper — has gone dark.
You climb it one WORLD at a time.
Every world is a course to run and jump through. Glowing SKILL ORBS sit on
the ledges — reach one and it teaches you a command, then drops you onto a
real prompt to try it on. Take them all and the world's TRIAL unlocks: an
actual problem you solve with exactly those skills. Pass it and the PORTAL
to the next world opens.
Run: A D or arrows.   Jump: Space or W.   Act at a console/portal: E.
Fall in a pit and you just climb back out. Climb all the way to root.

worlds.name: World 1 — The Filesystem
worlds.subtitle: look, read, and run
intro: You wake at a cold prompt. East, a blast door seals the way — beside it a
keycard script someone dropped. It won't run as it is.
Collect the three skills, then make the keycard run.

orbs.teaches: list what's in a folder; `ls -l` also shows each file's permissions
print a file's contents to the screen so you can read it
change a file's permissions; `+x` adds the 'execute' bit so it can run

trial.name: The Rusted Gate
trial.objective: Make keycard.sh runnable and run it to open the gate.

lines: # Emergency keycard. Run me to open the east gate.
echo 'keycard accepted — the gate grinds open'

hints: Look first: `ls -l keycard.sh`. Compared to a program you can run, it's missing the `x` (execute) letter.
Add the execute bit: `chmod +x keycard.sh`.
Then run it from here: `./keycard.sh`  (the `./` means 'the file in this directory').
learned: `chmod +x file` adds the execute bit, so a program is allowed to run.
`./file` runs a program that lives in the current directory.

reactions.say: Reading the script won't run it. Check its permissions with `ls -l keycard.sh` — the missing letter is `x`. Add it: `chmod +x keycard.sh`.

worlds.name: World 2 — The Log Swamp
worlds.subtitle: filter the flood with grep
intro: The floor turns to churning logs — thousands of lines pour through
/var/log. Somewhere in the flood, an intruder hammers a login over and
over. Learn to filter, then name them.

orbs.teaches: keep only the lines that match a pattern — your net in a flood of text
sort lines; feed it counts and it orders them
collapse repeats; `uniq -c` counts how often each line occurs

trial.name: The Flood
trial.objective: Name the intruder drowning /var/log/auth.log with failed logins, and write just that name into ~/intel.txt.
hints: Don't scroll 4000 lines. Filter to the failures: `grep 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log`.
One name repeats far more than the rest. Count them: pipe into `grep -o 'for [a-z]*' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`.
The name is 'wraith'. Record it: `echo wraith > ~/intel.txt`.
learned: `grep PATTERN file` keeps only lines that match. A pipe `|` feeds one command into the next,
so `grep ... | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` counts and ranks — the sysadmin's bread and butter.

reactions.say: That's thousands of lines — don't read them, filter them. `grep 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log` keeps only the failures.

worlds.name: World 3 — The Process Foundry
worlds.subtitle: see what runs, stop what steals

orbs.teaches: list running programs (processes) with their PID and CPU use
a live view of processes, sorted by who's using the most CPU
stop a process by its PID (the number ps shows)

intro: Heat rolls off the CPU cores — one is pinned at 99%. Something is burning
cycles it never earned. Learn to read the process table, then stop the thief
without harming the honest workers.

trial.name: The Miner
trial.objective: A rogue process is devouring the CPU. Find it with ps and stop it — but spare the backup daemon.
hints: See what's running and who's greedy: `ps aux`. The thief burns far more CPU than anything else.
Note its PID (the number). Stop it: `kill <pid>`. Read before you strike — one process only pretends to be junk.
The miner runs './xmrig ...'. `kill` its PID. Do NOT kill the backup-daemon; that one is friendly.
learned: `ps aux` lists every process with its PID and CPU%. `kill <PID>` stops one.
Read before you strike — a name in the list isn't always what it seems.

reactions.say: That was the backup daemon, not the miner — the honest worker. The miner (xmrig) is still running; find it with `ps aux` and kill THAT pid.
You won't find a process with `ls` — processes aren't files. List what's running with `ps aux` and look for the greedy one.

worlds.name: World 4 — The Tangled Archive
worlds.subtitle: search a whole tree with find
intro: Shelves tower into the dark, packed with decades of files. The system needs
its backup config, but something buried it deep under /etc — in a hidden
folder a plain `ls` will never show. Learn to search, then recover it.

orbs.teaches: search a whole directory tree for a file by name
make a new directory
copy a file from one place to another

trial.name: The Buried Config
trial.objective: Find the file named backup.cfg buried under /etc, and copy it into ~/restored/.
hints: You don't know where it is — so search. `find /etc -name backup.cfg` prints its full path.
Make a home for it first: `mkdir ~/restored`.
Then copy it: `cp <the path find printed> ~/restored/`. Tab-completion helps with the long path.
learned: `find PATH -name NAME` searches a whole directory tree for you — even hidden folders.
`mkdir` makes a directory; `cp SRC DST` copies a file into it.

reactions.say: Buried means buried — and it's in a hidden folder, so a plain `ls` will never show it. Search the whole tree by name: `find /etc -name backup.cfg`.

worlds.name: World 5 — The Cutting Room
worlds.subtitle: slice columns, count the culprit
intro: Blades of light slice the dark. A ledger of every access to the machine
scrolls past — /var/data/access.csv — and one account recurs far too often.
Learn to cut a column and count it, then name the culprit.

orbs.teaches: slice out one column from each line; `-d, -f1` takes the first comma-field
order lines — the setup for counting duplicates
`uniq -c` counts each repeated line; add `sort -rn` to rank them

trial.name: The Ledger
trial.objective: In /var/data/access.csv, find the username that appears most often, and write just that name into ~/culprit.txt.
hints: Each row is `user,resource,action` — you only want the first column. `cut -d, -f1 access.csv`.
Count how often each name appears: pipe through `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` — the biggest count rises to the top.
The top name is 'nemo'. Record it: `echo nemo > ~/culprit.txt`.
learned: `cut -d, -f1` keeps just the first comma-separated column.
`sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` counts each unique line and ranks them — the single most useful pipeline you'll learn.

reactions.say: 600 rows is too many to eyeball. Slice out the first column with `cut`, then count: `cut -d, -f1 access.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`.

worlds.name: World 6 — The Dormant Engines
worlds.subtitle: find the service that crashed
intro: A hall of cold turbines — the machine's services, the daemons that keep it
breathing. One of them has crashed, and the whole floor is waiting on a
diagnosis. Learn to read the engines, then name the one that died and why.

orbs.teaches: inspect services: `systemctl status UNIT` shows if it's running or dead, `systemctl --failed` lists everything that crashed
read a service's log: `journalctl -u UNIT` shows just that unit's messages — where the reason for a crash hides
a service can be dead now yet still set to start at boot: `systemctl is-enabled UNIT` tells you which

trial.name: The Stalled Engine
trial.objective: A service has crashed and the floor needs it named. Find which unit is in the failed state, and write just its name into ~/failed.txt.

journal: nginx.service: Main process exited, code=exited, status=1/FAILURE
nginx: [emerg] bind() to 0.0.0.0:80 failed (98: Address already in use)

hints: Don't read every unit — ask which crashed: `systemctl --failed`.
One unit is in the failed state: nginx. See why with `journalctl -u nginx` (its port was already taken).
Record the culprit: `echo nginx > ~/failed.txt`.
learned: `systemctl status UNIT` and `systemctl --failed` show what's running and what crashed; `journalctl -u UNIT` shows why.
Reading a service's state needs no special power — but changing it (start / stop / enable) needs root, which you earn at the very top.

reactions.say: A crashed service isn't a file you can cat — ask systemd directly: `systemctl --failed` lists what died.

worlds.name: World 7 — The Severed Wire
worlds.subtitle: read the network, find the leak
intro: A lattice of glowing wires — the machine's network. Traffic hums along most
of them, but one thread pulses wrong: something opened a port and waits for
orders from outside. Learn to read the wires, then find the leak.

orbs.teaches: inspect network interfaces and addresses; `ip addr` shows this machine's own IPs
list open sockets; `ss -ltnp` shows which process is listening on which TCP port
look up a name in DNS; `dig +short name` prints just its IP

trial.name: The Open Port
trial.objective: A backdoor opened a TCP port and is listening for commands. Find the port number it listens on, and write just that number into ~/breach.txt.
hints: Don't guess — list what's listening: `ss -ltnp`. Most ports are normal (22 is ssh, 631 is printing).
One line stands out: port 4444 owned by `nc` (netcat), bound to 0.0.0.0 (reachable from anywhere). That's the backdoor.
Record just the number: `echo 4444 > ~/breach.txt`.
learned: `ss -ltnp` lists listening TCP sockets with the owning process — the first place to look for an intruder's foothold.
`ip addr` shows your own addresses; `dig +short name` turns a name into an IP.

reactions.say: A listening port isn't a file or an ordinary process — look at the sockets themselves: `ss -ltnp`. The odd one out is the backdoor.

worlds.name: World 8 — The Supply Depot
worlds.subtitle: audit what software is installed
intro: Endless crates of software stretch into the dark — the package depot. Before
the next upgrade, the depot needs an audit: exactly what is installed, and at
which version. Learn to read the shelves, then report a version.

orbs.teaches: query installed packages: `dpkg -l` lists them all, `dpkg -s PKG` shows one package's version and status
find a package in the repo by keyword: `apt search <word>`
see a package's details — version, description, dependencies: `apt show <pkg>`

trial.name: The Inventory
trial.objective: The upgrade log needs the exact installed version of `curl`. Look it up in the package database, and write just that version string into ~/version.txt.

curl.description: command line tool for transferring data with URLs

git.description: fast, scalable, distributed revision control system

hints: Ask the package database directly: `dpkg -s curl` (or `dpkg -l curl`).
Read the Version line — it's 8.5.0-2.
Record just that string: `echo 8.5.0-2 > ~/version.txt`.
learned: `dpkg -l` and `dpkg -s` query what's already installed and at what version; `apt search` and `apt show` explore the repo.
Reading the package database needs no special power — but installing or removing (`apt install` / `apt remove`) needs root, which you earn at the very top.

reactions.say: A package's version isn't lying around in a file — ask the package database: `dpkg -s curl` prints its Version.

worlds.name: World 9 — The Hall of Records
worlds.subtitle: track history with git
intro: A vast archive of ledgers — every change the machine ever made, remembered.
But the relic project in front of you is untracked: edit it and its history
is lost forever. Learn to keep records, then commit the relic for good.

orbs.teaches: start tracking a folder's history: `git init` turns it into a repository
stage changes for the next snapshot: `git add .` stages everything
save a snapshot with a message: `git commit -m "..."`

trial.name: The First Commit
trial.objective: Turn the ~/relic project into a git repository and commit everything, leaving a clean working tree.

~/relic/README.md.content:
# Relic
The last known-good boot sequence.

hints: You're already in ~/relic. Start its history: `git init`.
Stage every file for the first snapshot: `git add .` — then `git status` shows them ready, in green.
Save the snapshot: `git commit -m "initial commit"`. A clean tree means nothing is left unstaged.
learned: The flow is always edit → `git add` → `git commit`. `git init` starts the repo; `git commit -m` saves a snapshot.
A 'clean' working tree means every change has been committed — nothing would be lost.

reactions.say: Repo created — now capture the files: `git add .`, then `git commit -m "initial commit"`.

worlds.name: World 10 — The Far Tower
worlds.subtitle: reach another machine over ssh
intro: Across a dark gulf stands another machine — beacon-01, a relay tower. The
launch code you need lives over there, not here. Learn to cross the network
by ssh, then bring the code home.

orbs.teaches: create an SSH key pair — your identity for logging in without a password
log into another machine over the network: `ssh host` opens a shell there (type `exit` to come back)
copy files between machines: `scp host:path .` pulls a remote file to here

trial.name: The Distant Key
trial.objective: The launch code sits on beacon-01 at ~/launch.code. Bring that file back into your home directory here.
hints: Look first if you like: `ssh beacon-01`, then `ls` and `cat launch.code`, then `exit` to return. But reading it there doesn't bring it home.
Copy it across in one step: `scp beacon-01:launch.code ~/` (a remote path is written host:path).
Check it landed: `ls ~` — launch.code should now be in your home directory.
learned: `ssh host` opens a shell on another machine; `scp host:path dest` copies files across the network.
`ssh-keygen` makes the key pair that lets you log in without typing a password every time.

reactions.say: You're on beacon-01 now — reading the file here won't bring it home. `exit` back to the mainframe, then pull it: `scp beacon-01:launch.code ~/`.

worlds.name: World 11 — The Clockwork Loop
worlds.subtitle: automate with for and if
intro: Gears the size of rooms turn in lockstep — the automation floor. A hundred
log files need the same judgement applied to each, and no one has time to do
it by hand. Learn to loop and to branch, then let the shell do the work.

orbs.teaches: repeat a command over a list: `for f in *.log; do echo "$f"; done`
orbs.example: for f in ~/logs/*; do echo "$f"; done

orbs.teaches: run steps only when a test passes: `if COND; then ...; fi`
the condition itself — `[ -f file ]` is true if it exists; `grep -q WORD file` is true if WORD is in it

trial.name: The Sorting Engine
trial.objective: Each file in ~/logs may or may not contain the word ERROR. For every file that does, append its name to ~/flagged.txt — and leave the clean ones out.
hints: Loop over the files: `for f in ~/logs/*; do ... ; done`.
Inside the loop, test each one for the word: `if grep -q ERROR "$f"; then ... ; fi`.
When it matches, record the name: `echo "$f" >> ~/flagged.txt`. All together: `for f in ~/logs/*; do if grep -q ERROR "$f"; then echo "$f" >> ~/flagged.txt; fi; done`.
learned: `for VAR in LIST; do ...; done` repeats work over many items; `if COND; then ...; fi` acts only when a test passes.
`grep -q` is a silent test — true when the pattern is found. Loop + test is how one command handles a thousand files.

reactions.say: cron.log has no ERROR — it shouldn't be on the list. Start clean (`rm ~/flagged.txt`) and gate the write on the match: `if grep -q ERROR "$f"; then ...`.

worlds.name: World 12 — The Throne of root
worlds.subtitle: become root, end the impostor
intro: The throne room of the kernel. On the throne sits an impostor — a daemon
wearing root's face, kept alive by its own launcher in /opt/initd-imposter.
You've earned the right to become root. Take the throne.

orbs.teaches: show who you are and which groups you're in (like 'sudo')
run as root when policy allows; `sudo -i` opens a root shell. Collecting this orb earns you the right.
delete a file — powerful and irreversible, so aim carefully

trial.name: initd-imposter
trial.objective: Become root, destroy the impostor's launcher, then end its process for good.

lines: # I am always restarted. Remove me and the mask falls.
It relaunches itself from ./imposterd whenever killed.
Delete the launcher, THEN kill the process. Requires root.

hints: As a mere user you can't touch root's things. Become root: `sudo -i` (you earned it). Then look: `ls /opt/initd-imposter` and `ps aux | grep imposter`.
It respawns from its launcher. As root, remove the launcher first — `rm /opt/initd-imposter/imposterd` — THEN kill the process.
Full sequence: `sudo -i`; `rm /opt/initd-imposter/imposterd`; `kill 1313`. Stay root — the throne answers only to root.
learned: `sudo -i` opens a root shell when policy allows it. As root, `rm` and `kill` obey without question —
which is exactly why root has to be earned. Order matters: remove what respawns it, THEN stop it.

reactions.say: You struck it down — but its launcher still stands, so it RISES again. Remove /opt/initd-imposter/imposterd first, THEN kill it.

outro: Welcome to the other side of the prompt.
You climbed from a borrowed shell to the throne of the machine — world by
world, skill by skill — and held its most dangerous prompt because you
finally understood it. That is what sudo really is: not power, but
